note: A retrospective lithograph of a scene labelled 1833, published 34 years later. The left bank's tavern is identified by the wolf sign on a tall sapling pole. Two low gable-front volumes stand together, with a broad chimney head emerging above the rear part of the left roof and a separate slender pipe on or beside the adjacent roof. Neither visible head is drawn as a full-height stack standing against a gable wall. The print supports a roof-penetrating stack as inferred form; it does not supply an exact ridge fraction, stack dimension, surveyed footprint or location. The 1833 depiction is applied cautiously as an inferred pre-1835 form, not as proof that nothing changed by 1 July 1835. The pre-refinement inline model did not reproduce these two gable fronts. Neither the earlier parallel-gable trial nor the new L hypothesis warrants a matches verdict without actual rendered review. The same sheet shows Miller House at the right: its tall main block has a horizontal-log ground storey and vertical boards above, continuing into the gable, with three small upper windows over window-door-window. That appearance is a tier-5 form reading; board width, relief, floor-level height and plan dimensions are not measured by this record. T-2386 L re-reading corrects the earlier parallel-gable interpretation: the NYPL left gable roof recedes rightward, the right one leftward, and their inside walls meet at an apparent corner. An orthogonalL is a supported form hypothesis, not an attested plan or scale. The physical polygon and all metric choices remain reconstructed; alternate views/chronology and actual render remain open. The1892-labelled poster is corroborative inspection only: fresh Newberry Poole27 metadata instead says1935/Copyright Not Evaluated, so its reproduction is not a new cleared modelling source. Source credit,1867 rights basis and Miller reading are unchanged. T-2386 actual-render continuation reads horizontal coursing through both facing gables, a markedly screen-left-leaning sapling and rising cross-arm with a tilted suspended board. These visible categories can guide inferred form; no exact timber section, colour, texture, sign drawing, height, local station, overhang or metric/world coordinate is attested by the sheet. The new proposal retains the existing source credit/rights/date limits and requires another actual rendered comparison. T-2386 door/log-relief re-reading: the two entry apertures are dark/open-looking and the course faces show rounded/irregular shading with narrow dark recesses. These guide appearance categories only; no interior, literal measured cross-section, authentic colour/texture or original sign-device likeness is established.
what_it_supplies: A pictured roof-penetrating chimney head over the Wolf Point tavern, identified by its wolf pole sign.
Two low gable-front volumes and a separate slender roof pipe, which remain open modelling differences.
A depicted date of 1833 and printed United States publication/deposit year of 1867.
At right, Miller House with an exposed-log lower storey and vertically boarded upper storey/gable; its exact dimensions and unchanged 1835 appearance remain unproved.
what_it_does_not_supply: Coordinates, footprint dimensions, an exact stack position along the ridge, or stack width and height.
Direct evidence of the building's appearance on 1 July 1835.
A single camera that reconciles this drawing with every retrospective picture of Wolf Point.
